Instead:) Be7 8. Bb2 a5 9. c4 h6 (Finally giving the bishop a bolt-hole on the h7-square.) 10. Rc1
parent_comment: This is the key move which gives this line a unique flavour. Moving the knight to the b6-square looks strange to a classically trained eye, but modern engines have challenged such prejudices. The c4-square is always a weak spot in setups where White combines d2-d4 with a kingside fianchetto. Black frees the c8-bishop and restrains c2-c4 while supporting a potential a-pawn thrust of his own. Incidentally, ChessBase classifies this position under ECO code D02 (d-pawn openings), but it is almost always reached via the 1 Nf3 move-order. Alternatively:

parent_comment: A line that has been surprisingly popular in recent months. I am not quite sure why people play this as White ... one does avoid problems with the d5 pawn, and from f4 the sensitive d3 square is often monitored. But this line tends to work best for White when he manages to get his knight back to a circuit involving the f3 square. The distance from the d4 square allows Black to play for an effective c5-c4 more easily, since there is less or no danger of a knight arriving suddenly on c6. Ponomariov gets sufficient counterplay with just such a plan.

annotation: 1-0 Nenashev, A-Permiakov,V Omsk 1996.
parent_comment: I must admit that I have always found this system to be more logical at first sight than the more popular king walk to g2 - after all, black often gains counterplay in that variation because of the weakness of f3, and doesn't white usually play h3 anyway? This has been played, but not so often, and perhaps because Nenashev has done well with other ideas. This game is really just an example of how dangerous the line can be for black, and an overview of GM Nenashev's systematic success with the line. Another question that occurs to me is why white doesn't try to play with his Q on c2 more often, as in the g3,Kg2 lines - the critical lines there involve black seeking counterplay by converging on f3 (with ...Qa8 and ...e6 or as we see this month, ...f5!?), something which is not really plausible with white set up with h3 instead of g3.

annotation: So here we are. Black has two main ways of playing against b3: 1) ...Ne4 (at some point) with either . .. Bf6 or ...Nd7 to follow. ...Bf6 places pressure on the long diagonal whilst ... I have the feeling that option '1' above should be best but it is not that easy gaining equality. In future I would personally try out an early ...Nc6!?.
